title: I was wrong about dark mode
excerpt: The one where I give my website a splash of adaptive paint.
content_html:
Monday 9 Nov 2026

Apple invented dark mode again!

They’re calling the new feature Adaptive Dark Mode™. I’m learning that other browsers already had a similar feature. I assumed people relied on add-ons like Dark Reader (and millions do). Regardless, pushing what is effectively an accessibility option to the forefront goes a long way to help people respect it.

My dark mode

My site used to have dark mode but I wasn’t happy with my colour choice and implementation. I redesigned my site back in Feb and removed it. Later I experimented with colour themes which I’ve since adapted for alternate blog banners.

In that experiment I said:

Personally I prefer reading with a dark theme for long-form content. Dark is not my brand though and I don’t believe every website needs to support colour scheme preference automatically. A good browser has reader mode, I use that all the time.

“Just enable reader mode!”

What a load of rubbish. You have to understand that sometimes I just write stuff and I don’t read it back. This also contradicted my previous statement:

That said, in [current year] brands with a digital presence — all of them? — should have a colour scheme for both.

That’s probably more true.

Certainly websites must work for forced dark mode. (Any site forcing light only itself upon users should go straight to jail.) So either provide a dark mode, or be prepared to test against every adaptive and forced dark mode implementation, or just let your website look broken. Probably easier to design a dark mode then?

So that’s what I did, again.

Maybe you noticed? If not, there’s a toggle button up top. At the risk of weighing in on the conversation I’ve opted for a two-state single button. I default to system preference. The mystery button flips between light and dark. Want to return to system default? Tough luck! You shouldn’t have clicked it. Delete local storage nerd!

My code

Technically I’m using a registered custom property with container style queries because it looks like fancy modern CSS. Three at-rules!

@property --theme {
  syntax: "light | dark";
  initial-value: light;
  inherits: true;
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  html {
    --theme: dark;
  }
}

@container style(--theme: dark) {
  body {
    /* make it dark */
  }
}

Most of my light/dark theming is done by customs properties. The default light colours (A) are set on the root <html> element. A style query applies the dark colours (B) on the <body> element. For edge cases that don’t follow the A/B rule I can use one of two techniques.

Either a style query inside a specific component:

.Component {
  color: var(--theme-A);

  @container style(--theme: dark) {
    color: var(--theme-C);
  }
}

Or use the light-dark() function:

.Component {
  color-scheme: var(--theme);
  color: light-dark(var(--theme-A), var(--theme-C));
}

Note that I set color-scheme to make light-dark() aware of the user’s choice that might override their system preference. I wonder if I can do this once:

body {
  color-scheme: var(--theme); /* safe? */
}

Is that safe? Let me know!

It’s not safe to do on the root <html> element because browsers checks that for adaptive dark mode etc. I’ll stick to the verbose style queries for now until I’m sure.

There’s a sprinkle of JavaScript to use local storage for the toggle button.

document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--theme",
  localStorage.getItem("--theme") ??
  (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light")
);

It’d be better to use a cookie and a server-side template. My website is hosted on a static CDN and I’m not adding edge worker latency, so I’ll risk Flash of inAccurate coloR Theme (FART). My site only risks a FART if a user’s choice doesn’t match their system preference. A week into my Noscript November experiment I see most websites are prone to a big FART because they rely entirely on JavaScript to enable dark mode.

I’m not happy with my button using a hidden label. Bit of a design failure I need to address later. My original goal was to have multiple themes but I ran out of time.

At the risk of soliciting replies to a question I didn’t ask, I would like your feedback on my choice of dark mode colours! Do they look nice? I don’t care whether dark mode makes your eyes bleed (turn it off) or you absolutely must have a 4-dimensional toggle.

Elsewhere

Stephanie Eckles wrote about the same CSS technique I use. Dave Rupert has explored the light-dark() with color-scheme variations. I saw Una Kravets is using contrast-color() with style queries to do something extra fancy. Stu Robson has written in depth on dynamic colour schemes too. Sara Joy has a great CSS-Tricks article on the topic.

If you read this entire post in an RSS reader and never clicked through, what a power move!

content_html_zh:
Monday 9 Nov 2026

Apple invented dark mode again!

They’re calling the new feature Adaptive Dark Mode™. I’m learning that other browsers already had a similar feature. I assumed people relied on add-ons like Dark Reader (and millions do). Regardless, pushing what is effectively an accessibility option to the forefront goes a long way to help people respect it.

My dark mode

My site used to have dark mode but I wasn’t happy with my colour choice and implementation. I redesigned my site back in Feb and removed it. Later I experimented with colour themes which I’ve since adapted for alternate blog banners.

In that experiment I said:

Personally I prefer reading with a dark theme for long-form content. Dark is not my brand though and I don’t believe every website needs to support colour scheme preference automatically. A good browser has reader mode, I use that all the time.

“Just enable reader mode!”

What a load of rubbish. You have to understand that sometimes I just write stuff and I don’t read it back. This also contradicted my previous statement:

That said, in [current year] brands with a digital presence — all of them? — should have a colour scheme for both.

That’s probably more true.

Certainly websites must work for forced dark mode. (Any site forcing light only itself upon users should go straight to jail.) So either provide a dark mode, or be prepared to test against every adaptive and forced dark mode implementation, or just let your website look broken. Probably easier to design a dark mode then?

So that’s what I did, again.

Maybe you noticed? If not, there’s a toggle button up top. At the risk of weighing in on the conversation I’ve opted for a two-state single button. I default to system preference. The mystery button flips between light and dark. Want to return to system default? Tough luck! You shouldn’t have clicked it. Delete local storage nerd!

My code

Technically I’m using a registered custom property with container style queries because it looks like fancy modern CSS. Three at-rules!

@property --theme {
  syntax: "light | dark";
  initial-value: light;
  inherits: true;
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  html {
    --theme: dark;
  }
}

@container style(--theme: dark) {
  body {
    /* make it dark */
  }
}

Most of my light/dark theming is done by customs properties. The default light colours (A) are set on the root <html> element. A style query applies the dark colours (B) on the <body> element. For edge cases that don’t follow the A/B rule I can use one of two techniques.

Either a style query inside a specific component:

.Component {
  color: var(--theme-A);

  @container style(--theme: dark) {
    color: var(--theme-C);
  }
}

Or use the light-dark() function:

.Component {
  color-scheme: var(--theme);
  color: light-dark(var(--theme-A), var(--theme-C));
}

Note that I set color-scheme to make light-dark() aware of the user’s choice that might override their system preference. I wonder if I can do this once:

body {
  color-scheme: var(--theme); /* safe? */
}

Is that safe? 让我知道！

It’s not safe to do on the root <html> element because browsers checks that for adaptive dark mode etc. I’ll stick to the verbose style queries for now until I’m sure.

There’s a sprinkle of JavaScript to use local storage for the toggle button.

document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--theme",
  localStorage.getItem("--theme") ??
  (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light")
);

It’d be better to use a cookie and a server-side template. My website is hosted on a static CDN and I’m not adding edge worker latency, so I’ll risk Flash of inAccurate coloR Theme (FART). My site only risks a FART if a user’s choice doesn’t match their system preference. A week into my Noscript November experiment I see most websites are prone to a big FART because they rely entirely on JavaScript to enable dark mode.

I’m not happy with my button using a hidden label. Bit of a design failure I need to address later. My original goal was to have multiple themes but I ran out of time.

At the risk of soliciting replies to a question I didn’t ask, I would like your feedback on my choice of dark mode colours! Do they look nice? I don’t care whether dark mode makes your eyes bleed (turn it off) or you absolutely must have a 4-dimensional toggle.

Elsewhere

Stephanie Eckles wrote about the same CSS technique I use. Dave Rupert has explored the light-dark() with color-scheme variations. I saw Una Kravets is using contrast-color() with style queries to do something extra fancy. Stu Robson has written in depth on dynamic colour schemes too. Sara Joy has a great CSS-Tricks article on the topic.

If you read this entire post in an RSS reader and never clicked through, what a power move!
